posts.quote: THE CHURCH BASEMENT COFFEE URN WAS THE SIZE OF A MAILBOX, AND IT WAS NEVER ONCE EMPTY.
posts.caption: After the service, everyone drifted down the back stairs to the church basement, where the big steel coffee urn sat on a folding table with a paper sign taped to it. The ladies of the kitchen committee ran it like a ship, and nobody ever saw them make a fresh pot. The cups were thick white ones that did not match, and the cookies on the paper doilies were arranged by someone with strong opinions. The grown-ups stood in little circles with their saucers while the kids ran laps around the support poles. By the time the last cup was poured, you could not have said whether the whole thing was about church or coffee, and it was probably both.
posts.first: My grandmother was on the kitchen committee for thirty years and she kept her own cup on a hook behind the door. Nobody else was allowed to use it, and nobody ever asked why. When she passed, the cup was still on that hook.

posts.quote: THE EGG MONEY WENT IN A COFFEE CAN, AND THAT COFFEE CAN KNEW EVERYTHING ABOUT THIS FAMILY.
posts.caption: Every Saturday morning Grandma carried the egg basket to the neighbors and the little grocery on the county road. What the eggs brought in went into a red coffee can on the top shelf of the pantry, behind the flour. That can paid for school shoes, a new belt for the washing machine, and one very unexpected birthday bicycle. Nobody was told how much was in it, and nobody dared to ask. She counted it at the kitchen table with the radio off, and she wrote the total on a scrap of paper that she then burned in the stove.
posts.first: My aunt found that can after the farm sold, and it still had a few coins in it and one folded dollar. She kept the dollar. I think she has it in a drawer to this day.

posts.quote: The good scissors were kept hidden, and everyone in the house knew the penalty for using them on paper.
posts.first: Ours lived in my mother's sewing basket under a folded scrap of flannel. She could tell from across the room if somebody had cut a magazine with them. I still cannot trim anything but fabric with a good pair.

posts.quote: THE CANDY CASE WAS BUILT AT KID HEIGHT, AND THE NOSE PRINTS ON THE GLASS WERE THE PROOF.
posts.caption: The corner store kept its candy in a low glass case right by the register, and anybody over four feet tall had to bend to look. Every kid in the neighborhood knew the layout by heart, from the licorice whips at the left to the wax lips at the far end. The glass was always smudged with the tip of a nose and a few small fingerprints that never got wiped off for long. You came in with a nickel clutched so tight it left a mark on your palm, and you stood there for a full five minutes. The storekeeper never rushed you, because he knew the decision was the best part.
posts.first: I once stood at one of those cases so long that the storekeeper pulled up a stool and sat down to wait with me. I picked a root beer barrel and a pack of gum, and I changed my mind twice on the way out the door. He let me trade without a word.

posts.quote: THE TEACHER KEPT A DRAWER OF EVERYTHING SHE TOOK AWAY, AND ON THE LAST DAY OF JUNE EVERY KID GOT IT BACK.
posts.caption: Mrs. Alder had a wide bottom drawer in her desk that stayed locked all year. If your yo-yo, your rubber band ball or your comic book went in there, it stayed in there, and no begging could shake it loose. The whole class pretended to forget the drawer existed until the final afternoon of school. Then she would unlock it, pull out everything one at a time, and call your name like she was handing out prizes. You got your marbles back, your pocketknife was not in there, and somehow nobody was ever really mad at her.
posts.first: I got back a harmonica that I had completely forgotten losing. Mrs. Alder had polished it. She said nothing, just handed it over and moved on to the next name.

posts.quote: THE BOOKMOBILE / A LIBRARY ON WHEELS, A DATE STAMP, AND A TWO-WEEK DUE DATE
posts.caption: Once a month a big square truck turned onto the gravel road and parked at the crossroads store. The back doors folded open and there it was, a tiny library with shelves bolted to the walls and a woman at a small desk with a date stamp. People came from miles around with stacks of books under their arms and a list of what they hoped had come in. You could take out as many as you could carry, and the stamp came down on the card with a thunk that meant you were responsible. Then the doors closed, the truck rolled away, and you spent four weeks rationing what you had.
posts.first: I read the same Zane Grey three times because the second one never came in. The woman at the desk started saving the new arrivals under the counter for me, which I did not understand then. I do now.

posts.quote: THE SCREEN DOOR HAD A SPRING THAT SANG, AND EVERY MOTHER KNEW EXACTLY WHICH KID HAD LET IT SLAM.
posts.caption: There was a particular sound that screen door made, a long stretched twang followed by a flat clap against the frame. It meant someone had run out without catching it, and the whole house knew about it. From the kitchen your mother could name the guilty party before the echo died. The mesh in the bottom corner had a little patch where a dog had pushed through one July, and the hook and eye never quite lined up. On hot days it was propped open with a brick and every fly in the county considered himself invited.
posts.first: Ours had a hand-painted ladybug on the screen that my sister drew, and it faded a little more every summer. I still hear that twang in my head whenever a door closes too fast. My mother never once raised her voice about it, she just said my name.

posts.quote: DAD'S THERMOS CAP DOUBLED AS HIS CUP, AND YOU WERE ALLOWED EXACTLY ONE SIP.
posts.caption: At six in the morning in the cold garage, Dad unscrewed the red cap from his steel thermos and poured a cup of coffee that was too hot to hold. Steam rolled off it like a small locomotive. You stood beside him in your robe and he would tilt it toward you without a word, just a quarter inch. One sip was all you got, and it tasted like burnt toast and grown-up life. Then he screwed the cap back on, checked his watch, and went to work.
posts.first: I did not like coffee for another twenty years, but I never turned down that sip. The thermos is on a shelf in my garage now, dented on one side where it fell off a truck in 1974. I do not drink from it. I just like knowing it is there.

posts.quote: Grandpa kept his pocketknife in the left pocket, his handkerchief in the right, and neither was ever lent out.
posts.first: He had a system and he never broke it. When I got my first pocketknife at twelve, he showed me which pocket it belonged in before he showed me how to open it.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the watch repairman)
posts.quote: THE WATCH REPAIRMAN / A LOUPE, A TINY SCREWDRIVER, AND A TRAY OF PARTS SMALLER THAN RICE
posts.caption: His shop was two doors down from the dry cleaner, a narrow room with a bell on the door and a hundred clocks ticking out of time with each other. He sat at a bench under a bright lamp with a little brass loupe screwed into one eye. When you handed over a stopped pocket watch, he opened the back like a surgeon and went quiet. Out came a spring, a wheel and a dozen parts so small they sat on a tray like grains of rice. A week later he handed it back running, and the bill was less than you expected.
posts.first: My grandfather's pocket watch stopped the winter he died, and I carried it in to a man like that. He worked on it for ten minutes while I waited and wouldn't take a dime. I still wind it every Sunday night.
